Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, purely CT-based approach for automatically detecting and outlining tumors in

Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer's research demonstrated a degree of complexity, requiring the study of equivalent hermitian forms and a detailed examination of quadratic forms in up to n+1 variables. Additionally, he showed that in certain cases, conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) find equivalent representations to those found in the symplectic group over a finite field, thus establishing a connection between these fields and the theory of algebraic geometry. This thesis, now translated into English, serves as an early contribution to the study of Lie algebraic groups and lies at the forefront of research in the field. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster, utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data obtained from the VLT/MUSE. By distinguishing nebular spectra from stellar continuum and identifying residual emission from rejected candidates, the research team was able to create a comprehensive inventory of detectable planetary nebulae within these galaxies. The statistical analysis of detected planetary nebulae allows for accurate calculations of the expected frequency based on galaxy mass, resulting in a reliable distance estimator that can be applied to galaxies lacking comprehensive planetary nebulae observations. By applying this estimator to individual galaxies, accurate distance measurements to galaxies such as NGC 1374 and NGC 5128 are possible, and even to galaxy systems like the Milky Way through the analysis of high-resolution data from surveys like Gaia, providing a promising alternative for determining the distance to local group galaxies. Additionally, this method can be applied to a large set of galaxies observed through wide-field planetary nebulae surveys, significantly enhancing the reach and precision in the measurement of galaxy distances
